events.title: Economists confirm the recession has ended
events.description: In July 1983, researchers say the economy reached its low point the previous November. Confirmation comes after the turning point.

events.title: Coca-Cola changes its recipe
events.description: The company introduces a new version of its best-known drink. Many customers want the original back.

events.title: The original Coke returns
events.description: Coca-Cola brings back the old recipe as Coca-Cola classic after customers object to the change.

events.title: Five countries agree to work on currency values
events.description: Their agreement aims to lower the dollar against other major currencies. Currency changes can affect foreign investments measured in dollars.

events.title: Apple splits its shares
events.description: Each share becomes two. Owners have twice as many shares, but the split alone does not double their investment’s value.

what_happened_next.text:
August 1982 began during a U.S. recession, a time when the economy shrinks and jobs can be hard to find. Many people were out of work, and prices and borrowing costs were still a worry. In July 1983, a group that tracks the U.S. economy announced that the recession had ended in November 1982. People did not know that at the time.

Coca-Cola changed the recipe for its best-known drink in April 1985. Many customers objected, so the company brought the old recipe back that July.

In September 1985, the U.S. and four other countries agreed to help lower the U.S. dollar compared with other currencies. Exchange rates can change what an investment in another country is worth in dollars.

In June 1987, Apple split each share into two. Owners had twice as many shares, but the split alone did not double the value of their investment.

This story ends in August 1987. A stock market crash came two months later. In August, no one knew what the next years would bring or which investment would do best.

reflection.what_people_were_focused_on: People saw news about the recession and interest rates, fighting in Beirut, Mexico’s debt trouble, home computers, business rivalries, and horse racing.
reflection.what_actually_mattered: Different investments rose and fell at different times. The economy and currency changes were part of the story, but no single headline could show which choice would do best.
reflection.what_faded_away: News about an evacuation in Beirut, home computers, and horse racing soon moved on. Coca-Cola’s recipe fight also passed. Big headlines did not always tell people what would matter years later.
reflection.what_nobody_knew: In August 1982, no one knew when the recession would end, that Coca-Cola would bring back its old recipe, or how each investment would change by 1987. A later recovery did not make its timing easy to predict.

hot_stock_outcomes.text: Apple introduced the Macintosh in January 1984. Pairing Macs with LaserWriter printers then gave businesses a new way to make polished pages. The Macintosh SE and Macintosh II widened the range in 1987; second-quarter sales that year rose 42%. These new uses and growing sales help explain the company’s progress during a strong five-year investment.

IBM’s annual profit rose about 20% in 1984, but its early lead in personal computers attracted cheaper rivals. In 1987 it launched the PS/2 to fight back. The investment ended well above its starting value, while the new product showed that even a computer giant had to keep defending its business.

Diet Coke became America’s leading diet soft drink by the end of 1983. Coca-Cola then changed its main drink’s formula in April 1985, angering many customers. The original returned in July. The company’s strong investment result covered both a successful growing brand and a famous product mistake.
